questions.title: Cause of morphine's poor oral bioavailability
questions.question: What is the cause of Morphine poor bioavailability (25%) from oral dosing?

explanations.A: Correct. Morphine is well absorbed from the gut but undergoes extensive hepatic first-pass glucuronidation before reaching the systemic circulation. Only about 25% of an oral dose therefore becomes bioavailable. This is why oral morphine doses must be substantially higher than equivalent parenteral doses.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Poor bioavailability here is not due to poor absorption; morphine crosses the gut wall well. The loss happens afterward, during hepatic processing, not at the point of intestinal uptake.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Digestive enzymes in the gut lumen do not meaningfully destroy morphine before absorption; the relevant metabolism (glucuronidation) happens in the liver, not through luminal digestive enzyme breakdown.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Morphine actually slows, rather than stimulates, intestinal peristalsis, and altered peristalsis is not the mechanism behind its low oral bioavailability in any case.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Morphine's oral bioavailability problem is hepatic (first-pass metabolism), not a vasoconstrictor effect limiting absorption into the intestinal vasculature.

questions.learning_objective: Attribute morphine's poor oral bioavailability to extensive hepatic first-pass metabolism.

questions.title: Why a morphine pain pump improved chronic diarrhoea
questions.question: A 39-year-old man who suffered a work-related injury has chronic back pain. A morphine pain pump was implanted to control his chronic pain. Formerly, he had chronic diarrhea which is now much improved. What is the most likely explanation for this finding?

explanations.A: Incorrect. 'Improved motility' implies faster, more coordinated forward movement, but morphine actually slows transit; describing the effect as improved motility mischaracterises the direction of the change.
explanations.B: Correct. Morphine acts on mu-opioid receptors in the enteric nervous system, increasing circular smooth muscle tone and segmenting, non-propulsive contractions. This increased tone with reduced propulsive coordination is exactly what slows transit enough to control his previously troublesome diarrhoea.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Morphine increases, not weakens, anal sphincter tone, which helps retain rather than release bowel contents. A weakened sphincter would worsen, not improve, diarrhoea.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Morphine's GI effects work through increased tone and reduced propulsion, not through a change specifically described as weakened rectal balloon dilation pressure, which is not the mechanism being tested here.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Weakened colonic musculature would tend to worsen bowel dysfunction rather than improve diarrhoea; morphine's actual effect is increased tone, the opposite of weakening.

questions.learning_objective: Explain morphine's control of diarrhoea through increased GI circular muscle tone and reduced propulsive peristalsis.

questions.title: Opioid effect that resists tolerance
questions.question: Tolerance develops to all of the following actions of opioids except?

explanations.A: Correct. Constipation is a classic exception: it persists essentially unchanged no matter how long a patient has been on chronic opioid therapy. Most other opioid effects fade with tolerance, but this one does not. This is why chronic opioid patients need indefinite laxative prophylaxis.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Analgesia is one of the effects to which clear tolerance develops, meaning progressively higher doses are needed over time to achieve the same pain relief.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Euphoria also shows tolerance with repeated opioid use, reflecting adaptation in the CNS reward pathway, so it is not the exception being tested.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Nausea and vomiting typically improve (tolerance develops) with continued opioid use, often resolving after the first days of treatment, unlike constipation, which does not improve.

questions.learning_objective: Name constipation as the opioid effect that persists despite tolerance, unlike analgesia, euphoria and nausea/vomiting.

questions.title: Action NOT produced by opiates
questions.question: Actions of opiates in man include all except:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Constipation is a genuine, well-recognised opiate action, from increased GI tone and reduced propulsion via mu-receptor activity in the enteric nervous system.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Vomiting is a genuine opiate action, from stimulation of the chemoreceptor trigger zone in the area postrema. It belongs on the list of true effects.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Analgesia is the core, defining action of opiates, achieved through mu-receptor-mediated inhibition of pain-signal transmission. It is clearly a genuine opiate effect.
explanations.D: Correct. Opiates cause miosis (pupillary constriction) via the Edinger-Westphal nucleus, not mydriasis (pupillary dilation). Mydriasis is therefore the correct exception among these four options.

questions.learning_objective: State that opiates cause miosis, not mydriasis, distinguishing this from their genuine constipation, vomiting and analgesic actions.

questions.title: Condition where morphine is an appropriate analgesic
questions.question: Morphine is used as analgesic in patients having which of the following conditions?

explanations.A: Correct. Morphine is a standard analgesic in ischemic heart disease, particularly acute myocardial infarction, relieving severe chest pain and anxiety. Its venodilating action also reduces cardiac preload and myocardial oxygen demand. Both effects together make it well suited to this specific clinical setting.
explanations.B: Incorrect. In bronchial asthma, morphine's histamine-releasing and respiratory-depressant potential can worsen bronchospasm and ventilation, making it a setting for caution rather than a favoured indication.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Advanced age alone is not the specific clinical indication being tested here; elderly patients require dose caution with morphine generally, but 'elderly male patients' is not the condition that makes morphine specifically appropriate.
explanations.D: Incorrect. In biliary colic, morphine can raise sphincter of Oddi tone and worsen biliary pain, making it a less favourable choice compared with other analgesics in that specific condition.

questions.learning_objective: Identify ischemic heart disease as a standard, appropriate indication for morphine analgesia.

questions.title: Treatment of choice for heroin overdose
questions.question: A young man is with known heroin addiction is brought in the emergency in unconscious state. On examination, the patient has decreased bowel sounds, depressed respiration and pinpoint pupil. The treatment of choice for this patient is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Naltrexone is an oral, longer-acting opioid antagonist used for relapse-prevention maintenance once a patient is already opioid-free, not for reversing an acute, life-threatening overdose.
explanations.B: Correct. This presentation, coma, decreased bowel sounds, respiratory depression and pinpoint pupils, is the classic opioid overdose triad. Intravenous naloxone, a rapid-onset competitive opioid antagonist, is the emergency treatment of choice, reversing respiratory depression and coma quickly.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Diazepam, a benzodiazepine, does not reverse opioid effects and can worsen the respiratory depression already present, making it an inappropriate and potentially dangerous choice here.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Buprenorphine is a partial opioid agonist used in opioid dependence treatment programmes, not an emergency antidote for acute overdose; the oral route and its partial agonist action are both wrong for this acute reversal need.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise IV naloxone as the treatment of choice for the classic opioid overdose triad.

questions.title: Opioid 100 times more potent than morphine
questions.question: Which of the following is 100 times more potent than morphine?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Pethidine (meperidine) is considerably less potent than morphine on a milligram basis, not a hundredfold more potent agent.
explanations.B: Correct. Fentanyl is approximately 100 times more potent than morphine. This reflects its high lipophilicity, which lets it cross the blood-brain barrier rapidly and bind opioid receptors efficiently. This large potency difference makes correct dosing especially important.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Pentazocine, a mixed agonist-antagonist, is not in the same high-potency range as fentanyl; it does not approach a hundredfold potency multiple relative to morphine.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Meperidine is simply another name for pethidine, likewise considerably less potent than morphine, not a hundredfold more potent option.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Codeine is a weaker opioid than morphine itself (often considered a prodrug partly converted to morphine), the opposite of a hundredfold more potent agent.

questions.learning_objective: Identify fentanyl as approximately 100 times more potent than morphine.

questions.title: Morphine action that is the exception
questions.question: Actions of morphine include the following except:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Vagal stimulation is a genuine morphine action, contributing to bradycardia; it belongs on the list of true effects, not the exception.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Miosis is a well-established morphine action, from Edinger-Westphal nucleus stimulation, and is a genuine effect rather than the exception here.
explanations.C: Correct. Morphine is emetic, not antiemetic. It stimulates the chemoreceptor trigger zone in the area postrema, producing nausea and vomiting rather than preventing it. This makes it the correct exception among the four listed actions.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Postural hypotension, from histamine release and reduced sympathetic tone, is a genuine morphine action and not the exception being tested.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that morphine is emetic (chemoreceptor trigger zone stimulation), not antiemetic, among its genuine actions.

questions.title: Analgesic acting through opioid plus spinal monoaminergic mechanisms
questions.question: Select the analgesic which acts through opioid as well as additional spinal monoaminergic mechanisms:

explanations.A: Correct. Tramadol is unusual among opioid analgesics in acting through a dual mechanism: weak mu-opioid receptor agonism plus inhibition of serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake. This engages the descending spinal monoaminergic pain-modulation pathway in addition to the opioid system. The combination gives it a distinct analgesic profile from conventional opioids.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Ethoheptazine does not share tramadol's dual serotonergic-noradrenergic reuptake-inhibiting mechanism; it does not combine opioid action with this added spinal monoaminergic component in the same way.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Dextropropoxyphene is a conventional weak opioid agonist without tramadol's added monoaminergic reuptake-inhibiting mechanism.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Alfentanil is a potent, short-acting pure mu-opioid agonist used in anaesthesia, without any meaningful monoaminergic reuptake-inhibiting component.

questions.learning_objective: Identify tramadol as the analgesic combining weak opioid agonism with spinal monoaminergic reuptake inhibition.

questions.title: Diagnosis: tramadol plus fluoxetine, confusion, hyperthermia
questions.question: A 50-year-old woman on tramadol for chronic back pain is started on fluoxetine (SSRI) for depression. She develops confusion, agitation, tachycardia, and hyperthermia. This is most likely:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Opioid withdrawal typically presents with symptoms like sweating, diarrhoea, piloerection and craving, not the confusion-agitation-tachycardia-hyperthermia picture described, and she is still taking tramadol, not stopping it.
explanations.B: Correct. Tramadol's monoaminergic (serotonin/noradrenaline reuptake-inhibiting) component, combined with an SSRI like fluoxetine, raises synaptic serotonin excessively. This produces serotonin syndrome: confusion, agitation, tachycardia and hyperthermia. Recognising this drug combination is essential before prescribing tramadol alongside antidepressants.
explanations.C: Incorrect. She is not taking morphine, and morphine overdose would present with respiratory depression and miosis, not this confusion-agitation-hyperthermia picture tied specifically to the tramadol-SSRI combination.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome is linked to antipsychotic (dopamine-blocking) drugs, not to a tramadol-SSRI combination; the drug history here points specifically to a serotonergic interaction instead.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Anaphylaxis presents with urticaria, angioedema and hypotension from an IgE-mediated allergic reaction, not this confusion-tachycardia-hyperthermia pattern tied to a specific serotonergic drug combination.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise serotonin syndrome from combining tramadol's monoaminergic mechanism with an SSRI.

questions.title: Why meperidine is avoided for chronic pain
questions.question: A 53-year-old man is requesting meperidine for his chronic back pain. His physician is reluctant to use meperidine for the treatment of chronic pain because of:

options.E: likelihood that meperidine will be diverted or sale on the street.

explanations.A: Correct. Meperidine's active metabolite, normeperidine, accumulates with repeated chronic dosing and is pro-convulsant, lowering the seizure threshold. This metabolite toxicity is the specific pharmacological reason chronic meperidine use is avoided.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Poor oral absorption is not the concern driving meperidine's avoidance in chronic pain; the problem is what happens after repeated dosing (metabolite accumulation), not absorption itself.
explanations.C: Incorrect. While meperidine, like other opioids, carries addiction potential, that is not the specific, distinguishing reason it is avoided for chronic use compared with other opioids; the testable mechanism here is metabolite toxicity.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Patient noncompliance is a general concern that could apply to any medication and is not the specific pharmacological reason meperidine is avoided in chronic pain.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Diversion or street sale is a general opioid-control concern, not the specific pharmacological reason (metabolite accumulation and seizure risk) that makes meperidine particularly unsuitable for chronic dosing.

questions.learning_objective: Attribute meperidine's unsuitability for chronic pain to normeperidine metabolite accumulation and seizure risk.

questions.title: Safest analgesic for a patient with chronic renal failure
questions.question: A 65-year-old man with chronic renal failure requires analgesia for moderate pain. Which analgesic is safest regarding renal function?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Morphine's active metabolite, morphine-6-glucuronide, is renally cleared and can accumulate to toxic levels in renal impairment, making it a less safe choice in chronic renal failure than an agent without this risk.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Pethidine's active metabolite, normeperidine, is likewise renally cleared and accumulates in renal failure, raising seizure risk; it carries the same category of renal-accumulation danger as morphine.
explanations.C: Correct. Paracetamol is metabolised hepatically rather than depending on renal clearance. This avoids both the renally-cleared toxic-metabolite risk of morphine/pethidine and the direct renal-blood-flow-reducing risk of NSAIDs. It is therefore the comparatively safest choice in chronic renal failure.
explanations.D: Incorrect. NSAIDs directly reduce renal prostaglandin-mediated blood flow, which can worsen renal function further in a patient whose kidneys are already compromised, making them a poor choice here.

questions.learning_objective: Identify paracetamol as the safest analgesic for moderate pain in a patient with chronic renal failure.

questions.title: Analgesic with mixed agonist-antagonist actions
questions.question: Which one of the following analgesic drugs has mixed agonistic and antagonistic actions?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Heroin is a full mu-opioid receptor agonist, not a mixed agonist-antagonist; it lacks any antagonist component at opioid receptors.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Fentanyl is likewise a full, pure mu-opioid receptor agonist, used for potent analgesia, without any antagonist activity mixed in.
explanations.C: Correct. Pentazocine is a mixed opioid agonist-antagonist: an agonist at kappa opioid receptors, producing analgesia, combined with antagonist or partial agonist activity at mu receptors. This is a distinct pharmacological category from pure agonists or pure antagonists. It can precipitate withdrawal if given to a patient dependent on a pure mu agonist.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Naloxone is a pure opioid receptor antagonist, blocking receptors without producing any agonist analgesic effect at all, the opposite pharmacological profile from a mixed agonist-antagonist.

questions.learning_objective: Identify pentazocine as a mixed opioid agonist-antagonist, distinct from pure agonists and pure antagonists.

questions.title: Molecular mechanism mediating morphine's analgesia
questions.question: A 34-year-old woman was admitted to the emergency department because of multiple fractures sustained in a car accident. The patient complained of severe pain, and an intramuscular injection of morphine was given. Which of the following molecular actions most likely mediated the analgesic effect of the drug in this patient?

options.A: Opening of Ca2+ channels on presynaptic nerve terminals
options.B: Closing of chloride channels on postsynaptic neurons
options.C: Stimulation of substance P release from nociceptive nerve terminals
options.D: Opening of K+ channels on postsynaptic neurons
options.E: Closing of Na+ channels on presynaptic nerve terminals

explanations.A: Incorrect. Morphine's mu-receptor action closes, rather than opens, presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels, reducing calcium influx and hence neurotransmitter release, the opposite of what this option describes.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Morphine's classic postsynaptic action is opening potassium channels, not closing chloride channels; chloride-channel modulation is more characteristic of GABA-A receptor pharmacology, not the opioid mechanism.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Morphine suppresses, rather than stimulates, substance P release from nociceptive nerve terminals, since reduced presynaptic calcium influx lowers release of pain-signalling transmitters including substance P.
explanations.D: Correct. Morphine's mu-opioid receptor activation opens potassium channels on postsynaptic neurons, hyperpolarising the cell and reducing its excitability. This is one of two complementary inhibitory mechanisms underlying opioid analgesia. The other is presynaptic calcium channel closure, which reduces neurotransmitter release.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Morphine's presynaptic action closes calcium channels, not sodium channels; sodium channel blockade is more characteristic of local anaesthetic mechanisms, not the opioid mu-receptor pathway.

questions.learning_objective: Identify postsynaptic potassium channel opening as the mu-receptor mechanism mediating morphine's analgesia.
